name: Dataset Licensing and Provenance
blurb: What may lawfully be used for what, and how to tell.

points.desc: A dataset's licence covers the compilation; the underlying web text keeps its own copyrights. FineWeb ships under ODC-By while the crawled pages remain their authors' - which is exactly the distinction being litigated.
points.name: Licence and permission are different questions

points.desc: Whether training on copyrighted text is fair use is the live question in the AI copyright docket - NYT v. OpenAI, Authors Guild, Bartz v. Anthropic and the rest are tracked with current status on the lawsuit tracker.
points.name: The provenance disputes are on this site's own tracker

points.desc: The Stack gates access and runs an opt-out process for code authors; GPQA gates to keep benchmark answers out of training corpora. Access control is doing licence work that licences alone cannot.
points.name: Gating is provenance control

points.desc: Dolma ships a datasheet documenting sources, filtering, and decisions - the practice the field is converging on, and the reason fully documented corpora anchor this catalogue.
points.name: Documentation is the differentiator

reading.body:
A dataset's stated licence and actual permission to use its contents are not the same thing, and most of the 17 datasets catalogued here carry that ambiguity unresolved.

The licence distribution makes the problem concrete. Four datasets declare MIT, four ODC-By, one Apache-2.0, and three carry no licence declaration at all. A licence on a compiled dataset governs the compilation. The underlying text, code, or other content retains whatever rights its authors hold, and those rights are precisely what the current wave of copyright litigation turns on. Seven of the 17 datasets carry licences in the CC or ODC family that are explicit about attribution and reuse conditions, but explicitness about the compilation does not settle the question of the source material.

The field has developed two practical responses. Gating restricts who can obtain a copy, and in some cases, as with code corpora, pairs access with an opt-out mechanism for original authors. Documentation records what went in, how it was filtered, and why, so that downstream users can make their own legal and ethical assessments. Both approaches are attempts to manage provenance without waiting for courts to define what training on web-scraped text actually requires. The litigation referenced in the data is ongoing, which means the legal boundary these practices are trying to anticipate has not yet been drawn.

What the data does not cover: it does not assess the actual legal exposure of any specific dataset, report the outcomes of any lawsuit, or address what happens to models already trained on corpora whose status is now disputed.
